title: Attention
theme: What do I notice, and what do I merely assume?
move: Use a staff-approved short local route. Record ten observations, three inferences and one uncertainty. Read legend, scale and orientation at three agreed stops. Practise posture, spacing, footwork and a verbal stop cue with a coach. Use solo movement before any paired task.
think: Plato, Apology 29d-30b and 38a (Jowett); Laozi, Tao Te Ching 1, 2 and 11 (Legge). Discuss: Can naming and examining a good life also narrow it?
make: Measure a paper map segment or ordinary classroom object five times using two methods. Record instrument resolution, units and the raw values. Compare the mean and range; explain why repeatability alone does not establish accuracy.
give: Agree a revisable group charter on evidence, consent and care.
prompt: What do I notice, and what do I merely assume? Write an initial answer, the strongest objection and a revised claim. Use a named passage or observed evidence; distinguish what you know from what you assume.

title: Discipline
theme: When does restraint make us stronger?
move: At a reserved serviced campsite, practise shelter setup, layout, dry storage and shared chores. The lead teaches the site’s actual food and wildlife procedures. Use staff-approved cooking equipment only. On suitable mats, use coach-chosen low-resistance balance tasks; no throws or submissions. Partners continuously agree the level of contact.
think: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.1-6 (Ross); Analects 2.4, 4.17, 12.1 and 15.24 (Legge). Discuss: When does repeated action become character, and when does it become conformity?
make: Use a short ruler or beam and small known masses over a low tray. Predict and test balance at marked distances from a support. Draw the force diagram, include the beam’s weight if material, and compare prediction with observation.
give: Make a fictional resource budget and explain one opportunity cost.
evidence: First camp review; balanced practice plan; opportunity-cost account.
prompt: When does restraint make us stronger? Write an initial answer, the strongest objection and a revised claim. Use a named passage or observed evidence; distinguish what you know from what you assume.

title: Evidence
move: Choose an approved route with simple observation stops. Measure sections against the printed map; explain why pace, grade and weather change a time estimate. Watch a short technical demonstration and distinguish what was seen from what was inferred. Practise the selected correction slowly.
think: Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section IV, Parts I and II; select a passage on causal inference and experience. Discuss: Why expect a pattern to continue?
make: Suspend a small soft bob from a secure low support. Use a small release angle and keep clear of its path. Time ten swings at three measured lengths with repeated trials. Define length from pivot to bob centre. Compare predictions made before measuring.
give: Give a peer one precise criticism that improves an experiment.
evidence: Repeatable experiment; uncertainty record; revised claim.
prompt: What would change my mind? Write an initial answer, the strongest objection and a revised claim. Use a named passage or observed evidence; distinguish what you know from what you assume.

title: Freedom
move: Pairs explain the next short section while the guide retains control. Rotate leader, navigator, companion-check and recorder roles. Keep the party together. Rehearse assertive verbal boundaries, stepping away and seeking help through non-contact scenarios. No simulated ambush or coercive role-play.
think: Mill, On Liberty, Chapter II; Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter II. Discuss: Who gets the education, independence and standing needed to speak freely?
make: Use a printed 100-cell grid with marked regions. Compare a convenience sample with numbers selected from a prepared random-number sheet. Estimate the proportion marked, then reveal the full count. Explain selection bias and small-sample variation.
give: Audit an instructor-written claim card, then propose a useful paper artifact.
evidence: Structured debate; printed-claim audit; capstone proposal.
prompt: What makes disagreement productive? Write an initial answer, the strongest objection and a revised claim. Use a named passage or observed evidence; distinguish what you know from what you assume.

title: Responsibility
theme: What do I owe to a place and to other people?
move: Repeat the readiness gate. Set up in a reserved serviced site; assign fair chores, verify communications and practise the agreed regroup location. Design a short safe sequence from previously approved movements, then have the coach review it before practice.
think: Tagore, Gitanjali, poems 35 and 36; E. Pauline Johnson, Legends of Vancouver, author’s foreword and “The Siwash Rock.” Discuss: How can a place make claims on our imagination and our conduct?
make: Use a synthetic route card with a specified mass, elevation gain and time. Calculate gravitational potential-energy change. Compare two routes for time, access and purpose. Do not measure or publish a peer’s body mass.
give: Test the artifact with a consenting peer or confirmed host and record a revision.
evidence: Two-night camp dossier; prototype test; stewardship evidence.
prompt: What do I owe to a place and to other people? Write an initial answer, the strongest objection and a revised claim. Use a named passage or observed evidence; distinguish what you know from what you assume.

title: Contribution
theme: What can I now explain, do and give?
move: Revisit a comparable accessible route or indoor map problem. Compare preparation and decisions with Week 1. Explain the difference between better judgment and simply better conditions. Practise the final sequence at an agreed pace. Show the solo or adapted equivalent. Include a stop and restart decision.
think: Frederick Douglass, Narrative, Chapters VI-VII; Epictetus, Enchiridion 1, 5 and 30 (Carter). Discuss: What can personal agency achieve, and what requires changing institutions?
make: Choose a question from an earlier lab. Submit a one-page design before collecting data: prediction, variables, method, equipment, boundaries and a falsifying result. Instructor approves scope. Gather a modest dataset and preserve failed trials.
give: Present the artifact and explain your individual contribution at the Jasper Commons Hearing.
evidence: Final portfolio; individual oral defence; 30-day commitment.
prompt: What can I now explain, do and give? Write an initial answer, the strongest objection and a revised claim. Use a named passage or observed evidence; distinguish what you know from what you assume.
